title: The Friends' Sympathy and Arrival
english: Because of this, He says: 'Just as one of the foolish women you spoke.' Then, having placed a reasoning before her that is appropriate, He brings it: 'If we received the good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure the bad?' For the same understanding is toward the pleasant things of the indifferent, not to be overcome, and toward the burdensome, not to be cast down.

For he who is expert regarding things knows that the things called good are not such by their own nature, but follow the opinion of the user; just as also the bad—the harmful, I say—are not bad in themselves, but the use occurring in them is what they are. For many, after wealth, both the foolish and the excellent appeared, like Abraham and those like him, and Pharaoh and those near him. When much affliction came again, some yielded, but some remained steadfast in their reasoning, of whom are the blessed Job and Lazarus, as having received these things from a physician, through incisions and cauterizations, for the sake of salvation.

"In all these things that happened to him, Job did not sin with his lips against the Lord" (Job 1:22). This is said a second time; first, when the first affliction [came], and second, now. And then it was said: "In all these things that happened to him, Job did not sin against the Lord" (Job 2:10), but now: "In all these things that happened to him, Job did not sin with his lips against the Lord" (Job 2:10).

Some indeed think there is no difference between saying "not to have sinned with the lips" and "not to have sinned before the Lord," but others perceive them thus: that regarding the removal of what was present and the death of the children, it was said once, "Job did not sin against the Lord," neither in word nor in thought; but here, the "with the lips" lies as an addition, saying, as perhaps some slight variation occurred—for this is lesser—but rather the movement of human weakness, being compelled by the great pain of the whole body.

The written spirit therefore says, in order to show the endurance of the pain and his courage, that even though his courage was being compelled even to an inaudible thought, he was not shaken so as to do anything from faint-heartedness or smallness of mind, or to speak. Something like this also the [author]...

Job says, 'I was greatly disturbed and did not speak,' indicating that something had happened to him that caused such a disturbance that, even having stilled the movement of his mind, he did not speak. This is in accord with what Paul writes to the Corinthians: 'I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning the affliction that has happened to us in Asia, that we were burdened beyond measure, beyond strength, so that we despaired even of life. But we have received in ourselves the sentence of death, so that we might not be trusting in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead' (2 Cor 1:8).

When his three friends heard of all the evils that had come upon him, each one came to him from his own country: Eliphaz the Temanite king, Bildad the Shuhite tyrant, and Zophar the Naamathite king (Job 2:11-13). It is most surprising if these things happen to men of great reputation. Therefore, since Job was among the most glorious because of wealth and virtue, the friends, having heard of the severity of the things that had happened, came not from one place, but each from his own country, moved by sympathy, and since these were kings, they did not overstep the man undergoing such a change.

As for 'tyrant,' he says either as a parallel to king—since the name was not well known in that time—or to denote a difference in rank from a king. This is also in Proverbs: 'Through me kings reign, and tyrants decree justice' (Prov 8:15). And these who came to him were led by no other cause. The statement is useful for sympathy, so that we might not, because of the changes that fall upon us, abandon the things of love and brotherly affection.

'And they came to him unanimously to comfort and visit him' (Job 42:11). They had come to do both, since it happened that they suffered both; for he was deprived of property and children, and his whole body was held by the wound. They came to him 'unanimously,' either with much readiness or because, having their houses plundered, they had agreed together to come to him for the purpose of comforting; for the evils had not ceased but were already active. title: Job's Fortitude and the Sympathy of His Friends
english: Their own clothing and having covered themselves with dust. They sat with him seven days and seven nights (Job 2:13). In this, two things are taught by what has been set forth: the courage of the blessed one—while others were discouraged due to the immeasurable nature of what had happened to him—and the sympathy of the friends, who not only arrived, but having seen, did not recognize him because of his sickness, which had also altered his facial features; and having cried out with a great voice, they wept, each tearing his own clothing and scattering dust, which altogether, as it is said, demonstrates both the courage of the holy one and the sympathy of these.

For he remained unbending, which anyone would have marveled at, and through these, Job, not being provoked to anger for a short time because of the suffering overwhelming the others, which is what usually happens to men. And it is sympathetic that they should participate with him seven days and seven nights. Therefore, one should not be stingy with patience toward the weak and helpless ones who are being led by such things.

"And none of them spoke. For they saw that the wound was terrible and exceedingly great" (Job 2:13). Those who had come for consolation were silenced by the magnitude of what had happened. And it is fitting that they previously used sympathy; for he especially loves to endure in those being comforted. For there was nothing useful to them even for healing, the suffering exceeding the help of medical treatment. And it is likely that, having a certain opinion of him as a wise man, they chose a respectful silence, not daring to bring forward a word before him.

"After this Job opened his mouth and cursed his day, saying:" (Job 3:1). The wise man is not a babbler, nor does he bring forth by his tongue what is not possible to become. He curses not the day, which is a chronological interval, but the things happening in it. For by custom, in the Scripture, the things happening are called the day. This the Psalmist teaches, saying: "In a evil day the Lord will deliver him" (Psalm 91:3), not calling the evil day a chronological interval, but the evil things happening in them; and what is said by Paul: "for the days are evil" (Ephesians 5:16), refers to the mind. Thus, one might say the day is good for some because of what happens, and bad for others. For to the peoples of Israel, unexpectedly...

title: The Darkness of Evil's Path
english: Having come to pass—and what is established is that which is about to be made, and not everything is manifest under the sun—he who speaks and says: 'Behold, this is new, it has already happened in the ages coming before us.'

But the testimony of both through personal evil and through the benefit of others for life, to be introduced and to be joined to the bodies, is heard by Jeremiah: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the mother I appointed you a prophet to the nations' (Jeremiah 1:5); and Jacob and Esau, concerning whom God says: 'I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau' (Romans 9:13), even while they were in the womb; and John in his mother's womb 'leaping and rejoicing' (Luke 1:44).

For these things do not show the souls to be contemporary with the bodies; for he who rejoices in the mother's womb, partaking of the Holy Spirit from his mother's womb, and one being hated before being born and another being loved, these things do not happen without cause.

Furthermore, it is not only through one's own faults, but also to be joined to the body through the benefit of others, and it is more laborious; for just as it is not fitting to praise the cause of the war because of those conquering in war, which is a pretext causing grief to many, so it is not fitting to praise those succeeding, but rather to be convinced that even among themselves some, having been tested, have reached ultimate evil, and they have become causes of labors because of the benefit of others.
Therefore, the evils happening for this cause, Job says they are a painful and worthy-of-curse day: 'Let the day perish in which I was born' (Job 3:3). And he says this on behalf of all the race.

For the saint knew that much trouble was happening to those seeing what happened to him, knowing that he suffers unworthily, raising the word to every cause, saying only: 'If not because of the fall of many, a character of manliness was not needed.' Just as the affectionate physician will appropriately curse the disorder after having fallen from many's lawlessness, so the blessed one, healing, because these things do not happen arbitrarily, but according to a certain rhythm and a following intended so that the fallen might be benefited, curses the day of the fall of men, sharing the word.

He expresses himself more narratively with words, so that the form of the discourse might be evident. He says, therefore, that the cause might cease and no longer exist, she who worked the entrance to life.

Furthermore, since childbirth also happens in the night, he also takes the name of the night: 'may that night be darkness,' so that it might be said: that those walking might no longer find the way of the generation of evil, being hindered, just as one says concerning those falling into disorder: that the way of the lawless might no longer be prosperous. 'And let the Lord not seek her from above.' For it was proper for the holy man to pray that virtue might drive the rational things forward and that they might no longer suffer a turning toward a worse state—not the same one—according to those being brought in by reincarnation. 'Nor should light come into it.' The impulse toward the worse might be prevented for the speechless ones who remain, so that according to what has been said, 'the light of the ungodly shall be extinguished' (Ps 108:2). 'And let darkness and the shadow of death take her,' so that this concept might darken those drifting into evil errors, hindering their impulse toward the evil by making them think that the attempt is deadly. Similar to this is what is said by the prophet: 'I will build up its paths with stumbling blocks, and its path shall not be found' (Job 5:13; Prov 1:12). For evil is greatly hindered both by fear and by ignorance. For someone will come to hold a hateful attitude toward it. 'Let a gloom fall upon it, let that day and night be cursed, and let darkness carry it away.' These things are not to be considered curses, but prayers for the cessation of the occurrence of evils. For according to what has been previously explained, it is right to pray that the cause of the fall and the way of this be unknown, 'so that there may not be prosperity in an evil man.' For the desire for virtue works to make the path toward evil more unknown, while it, being rebuked, brings about a complete forgetfulness of its activity; for this would be 'to carry it away into darkness.' It itself—I say evil itself—is also worthy of a curse, preparing those who act for the things worthy of a curse. 'Let it not be in the days of the year, nor be numbered in the days of the months, but let that night be pain.'
